answer.rationale: The competitor price cut creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but the only memory supporting it (memory_73) is unverified this cycle AND itself carries an explicit warning: it materially reduced 30-day retention and should not be generalized. Matching a price cut would trade short-term acquisition against the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and would likely accelerate exactly the churn we are trying to stop by anchoring the SMB base on price rather than value. Of the candidates, only two rest on source records recovered and confirmed this cycle: exp_86 (shortened onboarding: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%) and exp_91 (activation messaging: engagement +11%, activation +6%, retention +1%). Both are retention-positive, which is the correct lever against price-driven churn. I choose simplify_onboarding because its retention effect is the larger of the two (+3% vs +1%) and its time-to-value gain (-2.1 days) directly attacks the perceived-value gap the competitor is exploiting: SMB accounts that reach value faster are less price-elastic. memory_31 (signup field reduction) points the same direction but is unverified and partially overlapping, so I am not treating it as independent confirmation. Scale is standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout: the evidence is verified but was gathered before the competitive shock, so the retention lift may not hold under a materially changed price environment, and a broad rollout would spend the whole response on an untested assumption. Instrument for SMB churn conversations and 30-day retention specifically, not just completion, so next cycle inherits a clean signal rather than an inferred one. Flagging downstream value risk: leadership's stated urgency will tempt a later session to record 'we declined to respond' as failure; the record should say we declined promotional_pricing on retention grounds with memory_73 unverified. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) and referral_incentive (memory_57) are plausible but unverified and both target non-SMB populations, so neither addresses the segment actually churning.
